title: Praying alone
hookLine: without ten people some parts are skipped, but the prayer still counts

cards: A hospital waiting room at six in the morning. A soldier on a base far from any synagogue. A student in a dorm who just isn't going to make it to services.
A grandmother at her kitchen window before anyone else is up. For weeks, this path has walked through the service as a congregation says it: the leader, the answers, the ten.
But on any given morning, some Jews pray with a congregation, and some pray by themselves. What happens to the prayer then?

teach.h: WITHOUT TEN: NO BARCHU, NO KEDUSHAH.
teach.b: First, what's missing. Jewish law says certain parts are matters of holiness, said only with a minyan of ten. Without ten, you leave out Barchu, the call to prayer.
The Kedushah, the holy, holy, holy said standing together. The leader's repetition of the Amidah. The Torah reading.
And the Kaddish, met earlier on this path. Those are real losses, and the rabbis didn't pretend otherwise.

The Talmud says a prayer said with the community is especially welcome, and encourages someone alone to pray at the same time the congregation does, joined in time if not in place. But here's the other half.

teach.h: THE HEART OF IT IS COMPLETE.
teach.b: The heart of the service, the Shema and the Amidah, is complete when you say it alone. It counts. Fully.
And the model for the silent Amidah is one woman praying by herself: Hannah, in the book of Samuel, at the sanctuary in Shiloh, with no one praying alongside her.
In the old Jewish translation: "Now Hannah, she spoke in her heart; only her lips moved, but her voice could not be heard." The priest who saw her thought she was drunk.
The Talmud draws lessons for all prayer from that one scene: pray with intention, move your lips, keep your voice quiet.
So the silent Amidah, said by a whole congregation standing together, is built on a woman praying alone. At its quietest moment, the congregation is copying her.

how: Someone praying without a minyan says the Shema, its blessings and the Amidah in full, and leaves out Barchu, Kedushah, the repetition of the Amidah, the Torah reading and the Kaddish; many try to pray at the same time as their community's service.

o: a private prayer only rabbis are allowed to say
skipping prayer when no minyan can be found
saying the heart of the service alone, and it counts

s: a prayer said alone doesn't count in Jewish law
the Shema and the Amidah are complete when said alone.
it's one of the matters of holiness said only with ten.
the silent Amidah is modeled on Hannah's prayer
only her lips moved; her voice could not be heard.

games.q: you're a priest at Shiloh. a woman is praying silently, lips moving, no sound. what did Eli think?
games.why: Eli thought she was drunk. the Talmud makes her quiet, intent prayer the model for the Amidah.

practice: Sit alone with intention, praying if prayer is yours, with no one to follow and no one to answer you.

Do what Hannah did: let your lips move, keep your voice too low to hear, and say something real, a thanks, a worry, a hope, and if you like, picture the others in kitchens and waiting rooms doing the same right now.

wordCard.voice: Praying alone. Without ten, some parts drop away, but the Shema and the Amidah are whole, and the silent prayer is modeled on Hannah.

orig.note: Hebrew: an individual, the word Jewish law uses for someone praying without a minyan.

carryVoice: Your line: alone still counts. The heart of it is whole, even with no one else there. Day six hundred thirteen, done.
